subject: botany
question_text: Name the gymnosperms which contain mycorrhiza and coralloid roots respectively.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack botany section, Chapter 4 Plant Kingdom, book p.7, VSAQ 4. The book prints 'Corolloid roots'; the correct spelling, coralloid, is used here. Only one source book is held for botany — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand is physics-only and no botany board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card, not merely unrun. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Mycorrhiza — Pinus
steps.why: In Pinus the roots live in symbiotic association with a fungus; the fungus increases absorption of water and minerals. This is NCERT's own example.
common_mistakes: Writing Cycas for mycorrhiza — Cycas has the coralloid roots.
Calling mycorrhiza a disease. It is a symbiotic association; both partners benefit.
steps.memory_tip: Keep the question's order: mycorrhiza–Pinus first, coralloid roots–Cycas second — P before C.
steps.margin_note: Genus name plus one identifying phrase is enough.

steps.label: Coralloid roots — Cycas
steps.why: In Cycas, small specialised roots called coralloid roots hold nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria. The book spells them 'corolloid'; the correct word is coralloid — the roots look like coral.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'corolloid' as the book prints — the word is coralloid, from coral.
Writing that the roots fix nitrogen themselves — the cyanobacteria inside them do.
steps.memory_tip: Coralloid roots look like coral — the name describes the shape.
steps.margin_note: Underline the genus names Pinus and Cycas.

insider_note: The word 'respectively' fixes the order — mycorrhiza with Pinus first, coralloid roots with Cycas second; a swapped order loses both marks.
